output.title: Know the demo limit before you automate
output.body:
If you have tried ChatGPT but have not connected it to a real workflow, the first question is not whether AI can answer a prompt. It is whether it fits one recurring task in your business without creating more manual work around it. That is what demo limits are for: they mark the line between a proof of mechanism and a workflow you can actually trust.

For a small business, the right candidate is usually frequent, repeatable, already digital, and easy to measure. Think customer questions, lead follow-up, or invoice checks. The 8–10 hours a week example is only a persona frame, not a market claim.

That matters because a self-built demo only proves so much. Bareni’s knowledge assistant works end to end locally on synthetic Acme Shop data and approved documents, but the deployed public route is locked. The accounts-payable demo can block duplicate invoices and require human-only approval for risky steps, but OCR, billing, and three-way matching are not built. None of that means a business is ready to hand over money movement. It just means the demo stopped where the real boundary starts.

The practical next step is to check one workflow against three questions: is the output measurable, is the data already digital, and can a person approve the risky part? If those answers are still fuzzy, keep it manual for now. The gap between “I tried ChatGPT” and “this workflow runs on AI” is usually a boundary problem, not a model problem.
